name: Profile analysis (Ricketts E-line)

lead: The Ricketts esthetic line, or E-line, is drawn from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to the soft-tissue chin (pogonion) on a side-view image. Measuring where the lips sit against it gives you a concrete read on how full or retrusive your profile is.

Orthodontists use the lower-lip distance to the E-line as a standard measurement, and orthodontic and surgical planning use it. A published mean for lower lip to E-line is minus 2 mm with a standard deviation of 2 mm. Studies also show that preferred lip positions differ among observer groups.

paras: People take a straight side-on photo or use a lateral cephalogram, draw the line and see how far the lips fall from it. They use the result to decide whether chin or lip changes are of interest, and discuss it alongside other profile analyses.

This is a measurement convention, not a treatment, so it carries no physical risk. Cephalometric measurements are two-dimensional, norms are population averages, and preferred profiles differ among observers of different backgrounds.

angle.text: Forum users draw the E-line on side-profile photos to see where the lips sit relative to the nose and chin, then decide whether chin or lip changes are of interest. It is a standard orthodontic reference measurement. Preferred lip positions vary between observers and over time.

lead: The E-line, or esthetic plane, is a soft-tissue reference line defined in Ricketts cephalometric analysis as running from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to the soft-tissue pogonion. It is used to describe the position of the lips relative to the nose and chin, with the lower lip to E-line distance (Li-EL) as a standard measurement. [1]

Orthodontic and surgical planning use it, and studies of profile change after orthodontic treatment have measured lip position relative to esthetic lines. [2][3] Research has also compared skeletofacial morphology of faces judged attractive and not attractive, and studies show that esthetic preferences for lip position differ among observer groups. [4][5]
In looksmaxxing culture the line is used informally for discussing chin and lip balance; the sources reviewed contain little direct community discussion of it.
infobox: Soft-tissue nose tip to soft-tissue pogonion

paras: Wikipedia's cephalometric analysis article defines the E-line as extending from the tip of the soft-tissue nose to soft-tissue pogonion and lists Li-EL as the distance from the lower lip to the line. It names Robert M. Ricketts as a notable contributor but gives no development date. [1]

A study of 30 attractive and 32 non-attractive subjects compared skeletal and soft-tissue measurements from lateral head films, asking whether facial beauty relates to a specific skeletofacial morphology. [4]

A study with four panels of lay judges (European American, Hispanic American, Japanese and African) examined whether observer and patient race, ethnicity and sex affect preferences for lip positions in silhouette profiles. [5] Another study compared photographs with silhouettes for judging African American profile esthetics. [6]

Studies of soft-tissue profile change after four-premolar extraction orthodontic treatment measured how lip positions change relative to the profile. [2][3] A 2022 study evaluated fully automated cephalometric measurements from an artificial-intelligence platform. [7]

General cephalometric caveats include that measurements are two-dimensional projections of a three-dimensional face. Studies of preference show that ideal lip position differs between observer groups, so a single average norm does not describe all populations. [1][5]

Studies using esthetic-line measurements include orthodontic extraction cohorts of 160 patients [2] and later cohorts [3], an attractiveness comparison of 62 subjects [4], panel-based preference studies [5][6] and an evaluation of automated cephalometric measurement. [7] These are observational or rater-based studies, not interventional trials of the E-line itself.
